schema.title: Response Register V1 Auth Register Post

get.description:
The authenticated client's own chat threads, newest first.

Mirrors `GET /v1/pro/chat/threads` for the other side of the same
threads. Without it a client can only reach a thread whose id they
already hold, so "ask a photographer a question before booking" is a
one-way door - fine from the pro's inbox, unreachable from the client's.

Ordered and paginated on `created_at`, not `updated_at`, despite
last-activity being the more natural sort for a message list. A keyset
cursor needs a stable sort key, and `updated_at` changes every time a
message arrives - a thread could move across a page boundary mid-scroll
and be skipped or repeated. Thread counts per client are small (you chat
with a handful of photographers, not hundreds), so the ordering costs
little in practice and the pagination stays correct.

Guest threads (`session_id` set, no `client_user_id`) are not reachable
here by design: they have no authenticated owner to scope to.

get.description:
For the Messages badge: conversations with something unread, and how
many messages. Cheap enough to poll.

post.description:
Everything in the conversation so far has been read by the caller's
side. Either participant; nobody else, admins included - they have no
side to have read it from.
The app is open. Sent at most once a minute while in the foreground.

delete.description:
The app went to the background. Best effort - if it never arrives, the
key expires on its own.

put.description: Show or hide the dot. Takes effect on the next request anywhere.

get.description:
When a client could book this package with this photographer.

The same rule every booking path enforces (bookable_time), so a start time
offered here is one the booking request accepts. Gated like the profile:
signed in, a live photographer, the photographer's city open to clients.

The authenticated client's own bookings, newest first.

Each row rolls up booking status with the gig and payment status the
detail route leads with, because "where is my booking up to" is not
answerable from the booking row alone - an accepted request that hasn't
been paid for and one that's been shot look identical there.

The gig and payment lookups are batched across the whole page rather
than done per row. `_find_gig_by_booking_request` (used by the detail
route, where it runs once) loads every gig in the table and scans it in
Python; calling that per row would make one list request a full table
scan per booking. Here the gig query is scoped to this client's own
gigs and joined in memory by booking id.

The browsing home screen: several differently-sorted cuts of one catalogue.

One request rather than one per row, for three reasons. The city gate,
guest check and rate limit run once instead of five times - five parallel
row requests would trip the public_read limiter on first paint. Row
composition stays server-side, where the honesty rules can be enforced in
one place. And a row with nothing to show can be omitted rather than sent
empty, which the app cannot decide for itself without knowing why the row
exists.

Every row sorts on a column the index already has. No row here required a
new ranking, and any row that would have needed one was dropped instead of
inventing one - "top rated" is not here, because ranking_score is a
composite of completeness, portfolio size, gigs, rating and tier, and a row
named for rating that sorts by a composite is a row with a false name.

With `niche_slug`, the same rows narrowed to one niche: its page, rather
than a second endpoint with a second copy of these rules. Every row takes
the niche's membership rule and shows that niche's work, and the ranked
niche row the home screen shows becomes `niche_ranked` - a `niche:` key
there would render as a tile linking to the page it is already on.

The pro's own listing, rendered exactly as a client would see it.

Deliberately lives beside _cards_from_index rather than in the pro
module: a preview built by a second code path is a preview that
eventually lies. Works at any onboarding status - a pro who is not yet
live is precisely the one who needs to see what they are building.

get.description:
Gigs the caller is party to, newest first.

Scoped by participation rather than by role: a gig has exactly one pro
and one client, so `pro_user_id == me OR client_user_id == me` returns
each side its own gigs from one route, mirroring `_ensure_gig_access` on
the detail route. No role lookup is needed and a user who is both a pro
and a client (the common case - every pro registers as a client first)
correctly sees both sides.

The date range filters on `scheduled_start`, which is the field a
calendar screen orders by, and is nullable: an unscheduled gig has no
date, so passing either bound excludes gigs that aren't scheduled yet.
Ordering stays on `created_at` regardless, so the keyset cursor remains
total and stable across pages.

post.description:
A fresh presigned PUT for the same asset, for a retry.

A retry used to create a new asset every time, leaving each failed
attempt behind as an orphan stuck in `uploading`. A presigned URL still
must not be reused after a failed PUT, so this signs a new one - for the
same key.

Start - or, called again, resume - sending a large original in parts.

Calling it again for an upload already in progress returns the same
layout rather than starting over: that is how an interrupted upload picks
up where it stopped.

get.description: The parts R2 already holds - what a resumed upload can skip.

post.description:
Assemble the parts into the original. The client then calls
`/complete` as for any upload, so every check that runs there still runs.

What is assembled comes from R2's own list of parts, checked against the
layout agreed at start - every part present, each the right size, adding
up to the declared file - not from anything the client says it sent.
Give up on the parts sent so far, so R2 does not keep them.

schema.title: Response List Niches V1 Niches Get

get.description:
The pro's own portfolio, with thumbnails and niche tags.

The gallery previously had no way to list what a pro had uploaded -
only to tag an asset it already knew the id of - so there was nothing
to build a grid from.

What a client would pay, for a price the pro is still deciding on.

The public preview at /v1/pros/{id}/niches/{niche_id}/pricing-preview
reads prices off existing active packages, so it 404s for exactly the
pro who needs it most: one setting a price for the first time. This
takes the proposed rate as a parameter instead, and reports the cap
rather than enforcing it - the pro should see that they are over the
limit while typing, not when the save fails.

put.description:
What the pro charges per extra photo, per niche.

Previously admin-only, which made the onboarding pricing step
impossible to finish in the app. The platform's per-tier bounds still
win at charge time; the value the pro set is stored as given so the
response can show both, rather than clamping their input and leaving
them to wonder why the number changed.

get.description:
The authenticated pro's own booking requests, newest first.

Scoped to `pro_user_id` only. The client side of the same underlying
rows is served by `GET /v1/client/bookings`, which returns a different
shape (booking/gig/payment status rolled together) because the two
audiences are answering different questions: a pro asks "what needs my
decision", a client asks "where is my booking up to".

Price a selection without committing to it.

The client is choosing photographs and spending money at the same time, so
the total and the cost of one more have to be on screen while they decide,
and both have to be the real numbers. This calls `quote_selection` - the
same function `submit_selection` charges from - rather than reproducing the
arithmetic, so the screen cannot quote one price while Stripe takes
another.

get.description:
Totals across every completed gig, from the same figures each invoice
shows rather than a separate aggregate that could disagree with them.
Every completed gig this photographer has been paid for, itemised.

post.description:
Create the photographer's Stripe Express account, or return theirs.

Idempotent: an account id we already hold is returned untouched. A
second account would strand whatever onboarding they had completed
against the first.

A fresh hosted-onboarding link, minted per request.

Never cached and never reused: Stripe account links expire within
minutes and are single use. The client asks again rather than storing
one, and Stripe's refresh_url points back at this endpoint so a stale
link becomes another attempt rather than a dead end.

get.description:
What Stripe thinks right now, and what it is still waiting for.

Read live rather than trusting our stored status: the account.updated
webhook is what normally moves it, and if that silently fails to
arrive a photographer would sit at "pending" forever with no way to
find out why. This gives them - and us - a second source.

AcceptBookingRequest.title: AcceptBookingRequest
AcceptBookingRequest.description:
Optional body on accepting a booking.

Everything here has a default, so the endpoint stays callable with no body
at all - which is how every existing caller invokes it.

ApertureType.title: ApertureType
ApertureType.description: Whether a lens holds its maximum aperture across its range.

BookingRequestListItem.title: BookingRequestListItem
BookingRequestListItem.description:
A list row is the detail view plus the two fields a queue screen needs.

`expires_at` is inherited from BookingRequestView and is the response
deadline: a pending request auto-declines when it passes (see
`app.tasks.scheduled.expire_booking_requests`). `seconds_until_expiry`
is derived here rather than left to the client because every client
would otherwise re-derive it against its own clock, and a phone with a
skewed clock would show a photographer the wrong time remaining on the
one decision the product gives them a deadline for. It is negative once
the deadline has passed, and null for any request no longer pending -
a declined request has no countdown.

ChatThreadListResponse.title: ChatThreadListResponse
ChatThreadListResponse.description:
Cursor-paginated thread list, matching the convention in
`app.services.pagination` used by the other collection routes.

Note the existing `GET /v1/pro/chat/threads` predates that convention and
still returns a bare array capped at 200 with no cursor. It is left alone
here rather than changed underneath the web app, which consumes it.

ClientAvailabilityDay.title: ClientAvailabilityDay
ClientAvailabilityDay.description:
One day of a photographer's calendar, as a client may see it.

Open or not, and when a shoot of the chosen package could start. Never
why a day is closed: blocked time, other clients' bookings and a full day
all read the same, because none of them is the client's business.

ClientAvailabilityStart.title: ClientAvailabilityStart
ClientAvailabilityStart.description:
One time a shoot could start.

Both forms, because they answer different questions. `start_at` is the
instant, with the photographer's offset - what a booking request sends.
`local_time` is the wall-clock time where the photographer is, "10:00" -
what the client reads. An app that parses the instant gets it in UTC and
would show the time in the phone's zone, which is wrong for anyone
browsing from somewhere else.

ClientBookingListItem.title: ClientBookingListItem
ClientBookingListItem.description:
Summary row for the client's bookings list.

Carries the same booking/gig/payment status triple the detail route
leads with, so a list row and a detail header agree, but omits
`timeline` and `next_actions`: both are computed per booking (the
timeline is a second query for transitions) and neither is rendered in
a list. The detail route remains the way to get them.

ClientHomeNiche.title: ClientHomeNiche
ClientHomeNiche.description: The niche a home response is narrowed to.

ClientHomeRow.title: ClientHomeRow
ClientHomeRow.description:
One horizontal row on the client home screen.

`key` is stable and machine-readable so the app can special-case
presentation; `title` is what the client reads. Both are decided by the
server rather than the app, because what belongs in a row is a fairness
rule - "new photographers" must never quietly blend into "most
experienced" - and a rule implemented in more than one place drifts. This
project has already paid for that once, in pricing.

ClientProfileNiche.title: ClientProfileNiche
ClientProfileNiche.description:
One niche a photographer actually has work in.

Derived from the tags on their portfolio rather than from their skill
rows. `recompute_pro_niche_skills` writes a row for every active niche, so
skills say nothing about where someone works - a tab list built from them
would offer twelve tabs, ten of them empty.

ConnectOnboardingLinkResponse.title: ConnectOnboardingLinkResponse
ConnectOnboardingLinkResponse.description:
A single-use hosted-onboarding URL.

Not cached anywhere: Stripe account links expire within minutes and
are consumed on first use, so a stored one is a broken one.

GearFloorView.title: GearFloorView
GearFloorView.description: Where the photographer stands against the floor, and what is left.

GearVerificationView.title: GearVerificationView
GearVerificationView.description: One piece of gear, as its owner sees it.

GigInvoiceView.title: GigInvoiceView
GigInvoiceView.description:
One completed gig, line by line.

Every figure is computed server-side from the gig's own record. The app
renders these and adds nothing up itself - the same rule the pricing curve
follows, and for the same reason: two places doing the same arithmetic is
how they end up disagreeing.

GigListResponse.title: GigListResponse
GigListResponse.description:
Deliberately GigResponse rows, not GigDetailResponse rows.

The detail view attaches a payment summary and a ledger aggregate, both
of which are per-gig queries; returning them for a page of gigs would be
an N+1 on the most-hit screen in the pro app. A list row carries what a
list actually renders - status, schedule, money - and the detail route
stays the way to get the rest.

InvoiceSummaryView.title: InvoiceSummaryView
InvoiceSummaryView.description: Totals across every completed, invoiced gig.

MultipartPartsResponse.title: MultipartPartsResponse
MultipartPartsResponse.description: What R2 already holds: the parts a resumed upload can skip.

ProListingPreviewResponse.title: ProListingPreviewResponse
ProListingPreviewResponse.description:
What a client sees, returned to the pro who owns it.

`card` is built by the same function that builds the Discover feed, so
the preview cannot drift from the real thing - if editing a package
changes the price range here, it changes it there.

PublicReviewView.title: PublicReviewView
PublicReviewView.description:
A review as anyone may see it, signed in or not.

Deliberately without client_user_id and gig_id. Those let any visitor link
a client's account to a booking with a named photographer, which no client
agreed to. What proves the review is real is that it came from a booking;
the niche and date say which kind and when. Whether a reviewer's name
should ever appear is a separate privacy decision, not made here.

SchedulingPreset.title: SchedulingPreset
SchedulingPreset.description: How a package's bookable times are laid out - see bookable_time.

SelectionQuoteResponse.title: SelectionQuoteResponse
SelectionQuoteResponse.description:
What a selection of this size costs, computed by the same code that
charges for it. Every money field is a Decimal and serialises as a string
- a float here would round someone's bill.

SessionBlockInput.title: SessionBlockInput
SessionBlockInput.description:
One named block of a blocks-preset package, in the photographer's
local time. An end at or before the start runs past midnight.

TaxProfileView.title: TaxProfileView
TaxProfileView.description: What a photographer has told us about their own tax position.
